evidence.text: The first one came out red, covered with hair like a fur coat; so they named him Esau.
After this, his brother came out grasping Esau’s heel; so he was named Jacob. And Isaac was sixty years old when the twins were born.
When the boys grew up, Esau became a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while Jacob was a quiet man who stayed at home.
Because Isaac had a taste for wild game, he loved Esau; but Rebekah loved Jacob.
One day, while Jacob was cooking some stew, Esau came in from the field and was famished.
“Look,” said Esau, “I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me?”
“Swear to me first,” Jacob said. So Esau swore to Jacob and sold him the birthright.
Then Jacob gave some bread and lentil stew to Esau, who ate and drank and then got up and went away. Thus Esau despised his birthright.

c: Esau
Esau, the son of Isaac and Rebekah, was Jacob’s older twin brother (
), so named because his body was hairy at birth. His descendants were called Edomites (“Edom” meaning “red”) on account of his reddish color at birth (
), the red lentil stew he received from Jacob (
), and the reddish color of the land in which he settled (see

Esau was a proficient hunter who brought tasty wild meat to his father. Isaac enjoyed its strong flavor more than the mild meat Jacob provided from the family flocks. One day Esau returned home very hungry from an unsuccessful hunt, and Jacob persuaded Esau to surrender his birthright in exchange for food (
). Esau had little regard for his birthright and was controlled by his carnal desires (see
). He also married two local women who were not Abraham’s descendants (
), which may have fed into Rebekah’s favoritism toward Jacob and her idea about stealing the blessing of Isaac that was intended for Esau (
). Esau’s anger on discovering his brother’s deception prompted Jacob to flee for Haran. The brothers were reunited twenty years later when Esau demonstrated gracious forgiveness (

Esau was born with Jacob grasping his heel; this omen was interpreted to mean that Esau’s descendants would be subject to Jacob’s offspring. The subservient relationship between the Edomites and the Israelites began in David’s time (
) and continued until the reign of Jehoram (
). Following a rebellion in 845
BC
, the Edomites briefly gained their independence but were conquered again by Amaziah (796–767
BC
). They regained their freedom in 735
BC
and then remained independent of Judah.
In the New Testament, Esau represents the line of Abraham’s descendants who lacked the gift of faith and were rejected by God as recipients of his promised blessings (see
). Herod the Great was an Edomite.
Passages for Further Study
Infertility
With the apparent exception of Leah—and only then for a time—each of the patriarchs’ wives suffered infertility before eventually having children (
; see also

). Children continued the family line, helped protect the tribe, and provided labor. They ensured that hereditary property would stay within the family, guaranteed assistance in old age, and enacted the proper funeral rites. Infertility was therefore a crushing stigma for a woman (
), who understood herself to be created as a vessel of life (
). It was considered a denial of blessing, design, and desire (
), and it brought shame (
), ridicule (
), and vicious jealousy (
In the Old Testament, childlessness is a theological issue. Fertility is controlled by the Creator (
), who causes fertility and infertility according to his purpose and his promises (

). God often chose infertility as a precursor to the birth of a promised or unique child, marking the birth as God’s own work. Childlessness is thus a trial of patience that prompts prayer and faith (
). Abraham learned to nurture faith in God’s promise long before his child arrived (
). When a couple has been infertile, a child’s arrival is marked as a special display of God’s faithfulness and creative authority.

God’s delays are not necessarily denials, but they remind longing men and women to use trials for growth and to see children as a gift that cannot be taken for granted. A childless home can be filled with devotion to God as human expectations are submitted to his will. And for whatever reason, a couple may remain infertile their entire lives. God’s people must not isolate their brothers and sisters who are experiencing infertility but must surround them with love and support.
Passages for Further Study
Abraham

“By faith . . . Abraham obeyed when God called him to leave home and go to another land. . . . He went without knowing where he was going. . . . By faith . . . Abraham offered Isaac as a sacrifice when God was testing him” (
). These key events in Abraham’s life illustrate the faithful obedience for which he is best known.
God called Abram from the city of Ur to become the patriarch of God’s people. Abram’s family relationships are recorded in
. Terah had three sons: Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Terah left Ur with Abram, Abram’s wife Sarai, and Lot, whose father, Haran, had died. On his way to Canaan, Terah settled in the city of Haran (
). God had called Abram to a new land while he was still in Ur (
). God told Abram, “Leave your native country, your relatives, and your father’s family, and go to the land that I will show you” (
). God blessed Abram by making a covenant with him that included promises of great blessing, numerous descendants, and a new land (
). These promises later saved Israel from destruction when they repeatedly failed to keep their covenant with God (see

Abram left Haran at age seventy-five. Entering Canaan, he went first to Shechem, a Canaanite city between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal. God appeared to Abram near the oak of Moreh, likely a Canaanite shrine. Abram built altars there and near Bethel (
), proclaiming the one true God at these centers of false worship. Abram later moved to Hebron by the oaks of Mamre, again building an altar to worship God (
When God again promised blessings to Abram in a vision (
), Abram exclaimed that he was still childless because Sarai was barren (
) and that Eliezer of Damascus was his heir (

). This obscure statement is clarified by the Nuzi documents, discovered at the site of the ancient Mesopotamian city of Nuzi. According to Hurrian custom, a childless couple of means could adopt an heir, often a slave who would be responsible for their burial and mourning. However, a natural son born after the slave-heir’s adoption would supplant him. Apparently Abram had adopted Eliezer in this manner, but God promised that Abram’s own son would be his heir (
The hallmark of Abram’s life was that he believed the Lord, and the Lord considered him righteous because of his faith (
; see

). Abram was declared righteous not because he was sinless. On several occasions he failed to do what was right—twice he lied about Sarai out of fear, and he took the provision of a son into his own hands with Hagar rather than continuing to wait for God to act (
). But he consistently returned to faith as the fundamental principle of his life before God.
Abram was eighty-six years old when Ishmael was born to Sarai’s servant Hagar. When Abram was ninety-nine, the Lord appeared to him and reaffirmed his covenant promise of a son and of blessing (
), adding circumcision as the mark of the covenant relationship (
). God also changed Abram’s and Sarai’s names to Abraham and Sarah (
). Abraham laughed at the promise of another son (
). Shortly afterward, the Lord appeared again to Abraham (
) and again announced the promised son. This time, Sarah was caught laughing in disbelief (
). Abraham was one hundred years old and his wife was ninety when the Lord did “exactly what he had promised” (
). The long-promised son was born and was fittingly named Isaac (“he laughs!”).
The supreme test of Abraham’s faith came when God commanded him to sacrifice Isaac (
). Abraham obeyed faithfully, trusting that God would not thwart his own purposes (see
). Just as the knife was about to fall, the angel of God stopped Abraham and provided a ram for him to sacrifice in Isaac’s place. Abraham’s faith was complete (

Christians understand the sacrifice of Isaac as prefiguring God’s provision of his only Son, Jesus Christ, as a sacrifice for the sins of the world. God has fulfilled his covenant with Abraham through Jesus Christ, through whom the blessing of salvation is extended to all who have faith (
), making believers Abraham’s spiritual descendants (

). Abraham’s life shows that God is faithful and worthy of belief and obedience. The full import of God’s promise was realized when the gospel was preached to all nations and people from all families of the earth responded in faith (see
Abraham was called God’s friend (
). All who live by faith are challenged to live as he did, daily venturing into the unknown with trust in God’s guidance and sustenance. Abraham is one of many great “witnesses” to a life of faith (
; see
), inspiring believers to persevere in faith because we know God is faithful.
Passages for Further Study
Jacob
Jacob, the younger twin son of Isaac and Rebekah, struggled with his twin brother Esau in the womb and was born grasping Esau’s heel (
). God told Rebekah that the boys represented two nations and that the older son would serve the younger (
Isaac favored Esau, an outdoorsman; Rebekah preferred Jacob, who was happier at home. Once, Esau returned famished from hunting and Jacob bought his birthright with some red stew he had cooked (
; see
). Some time later, Isaac asked Esau to prepare wild game so he could eat and bless him (
; cp.
). But Rebekah sent Jacob to deceive Isaac into blessing him instead, and her ploy was successful (
). Jacob’s ruse was soon discovered (
), but legally, valid blessings were irrevocable promises (
). So Isaac gave Esau a lesser blessing (
), and Esau plotted to kill Jacob (
). Rebekah convinced Isaac to send Jacob away to her brother Laban so that Jacob would marry among relatives (
So Isaac transferred the covenant promises to Jacob and sent him to Haran (
). Along the way, God appeared to Jacob in a dream and affirmed the promises of land and descendants that he had given to Abraham and Isaac (
). Jacob worshiped the Lord and named the place Bethel (“house of God”).
At Haran, Jacob began to serve his uncle Laban (

). Jacob loved Laban’s daughter Rachel and worked seven years to marry her, but Laban deceived him by substituting his older daughter Leah on Jacob’s wedding night. Jacob worked seven more years for Rachel and an additional six years to acquire flocks for himself (
; see also
). Despite many hardships, he had thirteen children and became very prosperous.
After twenty years, God told Jacob to return to Canaan (
). Fearing reprisals from Laban and his sons (
), Jacob organized his caravan and left while Laban was away (
). Laban gave chase, but God prevented him from harming Jacob (
). Laban instead upbraided Jacob for leaving stealthily and for stealing his idols (
). Jacob let Laban search his tents, but the idols were not found (
), and Jacob became angry (
). Though their conflict remained unresolved, the two men made a peace covenant (
); the location formed a lasting boundary between Israel and Aram.
Jacob now faced Esau and God. When Esau came to meet him with four hundred men, Jacob sought God’s protection and sent gifts to pacify his estranged brother (
). Meanwhile, that night, in an event that symbolized his whole life, Jacob wrestled with a man who dislocated his hip and gave him the blessing he sought (
). God also changed his name to Israel (“God fights”).
In the morning Jacob met Esau and the two were reconciled (
); Esau was gracious and forgiving, and Jacob shared some of his blessing. Esau then returned to Seir while Jacob continued to Canaan. In Shechem, Jacob bought land and built an altar (
), then moved to Bethel and expelled all foreign idols from his household (
). God reaffirmed Jacob’s new name, Israel, and renewed his promises of land and descendants (
Jacob’s favoritism for Rachel extended to her son Joseph (
). Joseph's brothers became filled with jealousy and hatred toward Joseph—further fueled by Joseph's dreams (
)—and they sold him as a slave (

). For over twenty years Jacob believed Joseph was dead. Only after letting Benjamin go to Egypt in Judah’s care did Jacob learn that Joseph was alive and would be the source of famine relief for his family (
). Jacob’s spirits revived, and he moved to Egypt and joyously reunited with his favorite son at Goshen (
), where he prospered for seventeen more years.
When Jacob approached death at age 147, he arranged for the future of his family. He made Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan (
). He gave Joseph’s sons his prime blessing (
) and put Ephraim, the younger son, first. He gave assurance that the family would return to Canaan (
), then blessed each of his sons and prophesied the future of their descendants (
). He died and was buried at the cave of Machpelah, accompanied by his sons and a large Egyptian procession (
). His death marked the end of the patriarchal age and the beginning of Israel’s growth as a nation in Egypt until they returned to live again in the Promised Land (see Exodus—Joshua).
The name “Jacob” became synonymous with the nation of Israel (see
). God called the nation to serve him as their forefathers had done (
). He promised Israel the same love that he had shown toward Jacob (
). And he promised that a conquering ruler would come from Jacob’s descendants (
